sp101-m1.q: How do you say "Good afternoon" in Spanish?
sp101-m1.explanation: “Tarde” means afternoon, and greetings are plural: Buenas tardes. Use it from midday until it gets dark.
why: “Buenos días” is “good morning” (días = days).
“Buenas noches” is “good evening / good night”, used once it is dark.
“Hasta luego” means “see you later”. It is a goodbye, not a greeting.

sp101-m1.explanation: Literally “how do you call yourself?”. It is how Spanish asks your name, and you answer “Me llamo…”.
why: “How are you?” is “¿Cómo estás?”. It starts the same way but ends differently.
“Where are you from?” is “¿De dónde eres?”.
“How old are you?” is “¿Cuántos años tienes?”.

sp101-m1.q: How do you say "I am 28 years old" in Spanish?
sp101-m1.explanation: Spanish uses tener (to have) for age: “I have 28 years”. It is never ser or estar.
why: “Soy” (ser) says who or what you are (“Soy profesor”). Age uses tener.
“Estoy” (estar) is for location or temporary states, not for age.
“Me llamo” means “my name is”, so this would say “my name is 28 years”.

sp101-m2.q: What is the Spanish word for Wednesday?
sp101-m2.explanation: Miércoles is Wednesday. The week: lunes, martes, miércoles, jueves, viernes, sábado, domingo.
why: “Martes” is Tuesday.
“Jueves” is Thursday.
“Viernes” is Friday.

sp101-m2.q: How do you say "On Monday I'm going to the beach"?
options: El lunes voy a la playa
El martes voy a la playa
sp101-m2.explanation: “El lunes” is “on Monday” (el + the day, no “en”). “Voy a la playa” is “I'm going to the beach”: ir + a + the place.
why: “Estoy” (I am) does not say you are going somewhere; “voy a” (ir) does. The sentence is also missing the “a” before “la playa”.
Too much is missing: you need “el” before the day, “a” after “voy” and “la” before “playa”.
The structure is right, but “el martes” is Tuesday. The sentence says Monday (lunes).

sp101-m2.q: Which is the correct combination of "a" + "el"?
sp101-m2.explanation: “A” + “el” always joins into “al”: voy al parque. It only happens with “el”, not with la, los or las.
why: Spanish does not leave “a el” apart; the two words contract.
The order is wrong, and “el a” is not a form we use.
“Ale” is not a Spanish word. The contraction is “al”.

sp101-m2.q: How do you say "In August I'm going skiing"?
sp101-m2.explanation: Months take “en”: en agosto = in August. Then “voy a” + an infinitive means “I'm going to ski”.
why: Months do not take “el”. Days do (el lunes), months use “en”.
Two things are missing: “en” before the month and “a” in “voy a esquiar”.
“Estoy esquiar” mixes estar with an infinitive. “I'm going to ski” is “voy a esquiar”.

sp101-m3.q: What is the correct definite article for "niñas" (girls)?
sp101-m3.explanation: Niñas is feminine and plural (it ends in -as), so the article is “las”. Article, gender and number must match: la niña → las niñas.
why: “El” is masculine singular.
“Los” is masculine plural. Niñas is feminine.
“La” is feminine but singular. Niñas is plural.

sp101-m3.q: How do you say "a boy" in Spanish?
sp101-m3.explanation: “A boy” uses the indefinite article (a/an): “un” for masculine singular, so “un niño”.
why: “El niño” means “the boy”, a definite article, not “a boy”.
“Unos niños” means “some boys”, which is plural.
“La” is feminine and niño is masculine. They must match: el niño, la niña.

sp101-m3.q: Which sentence is correct in Spanish?
sp101-m3.explanation: After ser with a profession, Spanish drops un/una: “Soy doctor”, “Es profesora”. You only add the article when you add an adjective: “Soy un buen doctor”.
why: English says “I am a doctor”, but Spanish leaves out “un” before a profession.
“Estoy” (estar) is for location or state. Professions use ser, and still no article.
“El” goes with a noun, and here it sits in front of a verb (“el soy”), which makes no sense.

sp101-m3.q: How do you say "I don't have a car" in Spanish?
sp101-m3.explanation: After a negative “no tengo”, Spanish usually drops un/una when you mean “any” of something: “No tengo coche”, “No tengo hermanos”.
why: It is grammatical, but it stresses “not even one car”. The everyday way, and the pattern this module teaches, drops the article after a negative.
“Soy” (ser) means “I am”, so this says “I am not a car”. To talk about having something, use tener.
“Estoy” means “I am” (a place or a state), not “I have”. Possession uses tener.

sp101-m4.q: What is the correct "yo" form of "hablar"?
sp101-m4.explanation: For regular -AR verbs, drop -ar and add the ending. For yo the ending is -o: hablo.
why: “Hablas” is the tú form (you speak).
“Habla” is the él / ella / usted form (he, she speaks).
“Hablamos” is the nosotros form (we speak).

sp101-m4.q: How do you say "She lives in Barcelona"?
sp101-m4.explanation: “Ella” takes the él / ella ending. For the -IR verb vivir that ending is -e: vive.
why: “Vivo” is the yo form (I live).
“Vives” is the tú form (you live).
“Vivir” is the infinitive. The verb has to be conjugated to match “ella”.

sp101-m4.q: Which ending do -ER verbs take for "tú"?
sp101-m4.explanation: Regular -ER verbs take -es for tú: comes, bebes, aprendes. (-AR verbs take -as: hablas.)
why: “-as” is the tú ending for -AR verbs (hablas), not for -ER.
“-is” is not a tú ending. It only shows up inside vosotros forms such as vivís.
“-os” is not a tú ending either. Tú always ends in -s: hablas, comes, vives.

sp101-m4.q: How do you say "They eat at the restaurant"?
sp101-m4.explanation: “Ellos” (they) with an -ER verb takes -en: ellos comen.
why: “Come” is the él / ella form. “Ellos” needs the plural ending -en.
“Comer” is the infinitive. It has to be conjugated.
“Comemos” is the nosotros form (we eat).

sp101-m5.q: How do you ask "Where is the hotel?" in Spanish?
sp101-m5.explanation: The location of a place uses estar: “¿Dónde está…?” means “Where is…?”.
why: “¿Puedo el hotel?” is “Can I the hotel?”. “Puedo” (can I) needs another verb after it.
“¿Tienes el hotel?” means “Do you have the hotel?”.
“¿Dónde es…?” is for where an event happens (“¿Dónde es la fiesta?”). For where a place is, use “está”.

sp101-m5.q: How do you say "Can I pay by card?"
sp101-m5.explanation: “¿Puedo…?” means “Can I…?” and takes an infinitive: ¿Puedo pagar con tarjeta?
why: “Necesito pagar” is “I need to pay”. It is a statement, not a question about whether you can.
“¿Debería…?” means “Should I…?”. It asks what is advisable, not what is allowed.
“Vamos pagar” is not correct Spanish. “Vamos a pagar” means “let's pay”, and it is not a question either.

sp101-m5.explanation: “Tener tiempo” means “to have time”, so “¿Tienes tiempo?” is “Do you have time?”.
why: “Tiempo” is time (or weather), not money. Money is “dinero”.
“What time is it?” is “¿Qué hora es?”. Hora is the time on the clock, tiempo is time in general.
“Should I wait?” would be “¿Debo esperar?”.

sp101-m5.q: How do you say "Where are the taxis?"
sp101-m5.explanation: “Los taxis” is plural, so the verb must be plural too: están. Locations use estar.
why: “Está” is singular. The taxis are plural, so it has to be “están”.
“Son” (ser) is not used for location, so “¿Dónde son…?” is wrong here.
“¿Tienes los taxis?” means “Do you have the taxis?”.

sp101-m6.q: How do you say "It's sunny" in Spanish?
sp101-m6.explanation: Spanish uses hacer for many weather conditions: hace sol, hace calor, hace frío, hace viento.
why: In this module “hay” is for things you can see in the air, like fog or clouds. Sunshine uses hacer.
“Está sol” is not used. Estar goes with ongoing actions like “está lloviendo”.
“Es sol” would say “it is sun”. Ser does not describe the weather.

sp101-m6.q: Which verb do you use for "It's raining" (ongoing)?
sp101-m6.explanation: Weather that is happening right now uses estar + -ando/-iendo: está lloviendo, está nevando.
why: “Hacer” goes with conditions such as sol, viento, calor and frío.
“Haber” (hay) goes with things present in the air, like fog or clouds.
“Tener” is for having, age and feelings (“tengo frío” = I feel cold), not for the weather itself.

sp101-m6.q: How do you say "It's foggy" in Spanish?
sp101-m6.explanation: Fog is something that is there in the air, so Spanish uses “hay” (there is): hay niebla, hay nubes.
why: “Hace” is for sol, calor, frío and viento. Niebla uses “hay”.
“Está niebla” is not used. “Está” needs an adjective, like “está nublado”.
“Es niebla” would say “it is fog”. Ser does not describe the weather.

sp101-m6.q: Which of these uses the verb "hacer"?
sp101-m6.explanation: “Hace viento” (it's windy) uses hacer, which covers sol, viento, calor and frío.
why: “Está nublado” uses estar (it's cloudy).
“Hay niebla” uses haber.
“Está lloviendo” uses estar.

sp101-m7.q: What is the main goal of the Module 7 speaking exercise?
options: Describing a picture using everything learned so far
sp101-m7.explanation: Module 7 is a speaking exercise: you describe a picture using everything you have learned so far (greetings, numbers, places, verbs, weather).
why: The vocabulary comes from the earlier modules. Here you use what you already know.
You speak about a picture, you do not translate sentences.
It is about describing pictures out loud, not writing essays.

sp101-m7.q: Which would you use to describe weather in a picture?
sp101-m7.explanation: “Hace sol” and “Está lloviendo” are the weather phrases from Module 6, which is what you need to describe the weather in a picture.
why: “Me llamo…” means “my name is…”. It belongs to introductions.
“Voy a la playa” is “I'm going to the beach”: a plan or a place, not the weather.
“Tengo 25 años” is “I'm 25”. That is age.

sp101-m7.q: What happens to the picture practice as you advance?
options: It gets replaced with grammar tests
Expectations increase as your vocabulary grows
sp101-m7.explanation: The practice gets more demanding as you learn more: with a bigger vocabulary you are expected to describe more, in more detail.
why: It does not get easier. It asks more of you as you progress.
It does not stay the same: more is expected over time.
The picture practice is not replaced. It continues, with higher expectations.
